title: Your AI Product Will Fail Unless You Can Explain It - Veronica Hylak, Hey AI

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk is about how founders communicate AI products so humans understand them, which is a product UX and human-factors concern. The pitching framework applies across AI product verticals with examples from security, support, and general enterprise use cases. The content addresses the go-to-market communication challenge of making AI products comprehensible to buyers. The talk is accessible to non-technical audiences with no prerequisites and uses everyday analogies. This is a conference-style presentation delivered as a single talk. summary: Veronica Hylak delivers a focused talk on the communication gap that plagues AI product founders. She opens by contrasting a typical jargon-filled AI pitch—"agentic AI orchestration platform for enterprise knowledge retrieval"—with the reality that buyers disengage instantly. The core thesis is that technical excellence no longer guarantees market success; clarity does. She introduces a three-part fix. First, identify the wound: immerse the audience in their daily pain rather than leading with what you built. She uses a SecOps example, showing how framing exhaustion with disconnected tools creates emotional resonance. The format requires about 20 seconds: identify the wound, say "we fix that," then show how. Second, make the product click: apply the 17-year-old test. If a teenager can't understand it, you'll lose the room. She recommends tying products to viral stories people already know, like the McDonald's AI drive-thru failures, and banning abstract terms in favor of mental images such as "smoke alarm for AI behavior." Technical precision can come later in the sale. Third, show the transformation: prove value through before/after contrast rather than vague claims like "we increase productivity." She illustrates with a support-team example: 30 minutes of digging versus 10 seconds with sources attached. She closes by redoing the opening elevator pitch using the full framework, then invites founders to share their storytelling challenges in comments.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Problem with Typical AI Pitches
sections.summary: Hylak opens with a satirical agentic-AI pitch full of buzzwords, illustrating why buyers disengage. Founders ship fast but have one elevator-length shot to make their mark.

sections.title: Step 1: The Wound
sections.summary: Never start with what you built. Immerse the audience in their daily job and show what they are tired of. A SecOps example demonstrates how describing exhausted security teams with disconnected tools creates emotional resonance. The 20-second format: identify the wound, say 'we fix that,' then show how.

sections.title: Step 2: Make the Product Click
sections.summary: Apply the 17-year-old test. Tie products to viral stories like the McDonald's AI drive-thru. Ban abstract words no one can picture; use mental images such as 'smoke alarm for AI behavior.' Technical definitions can come later—they are not the front door.

sections.title: Step 3: Show the Transformation
sections.summary: Stop describing the product and prove its value through before/after contrast. Vague claims like 'we increase productivity' fail. A support-team example shows 30 minutes of digging replaced by a 10-second answer with sources.

sections.title: Elevator Pitch Redo and Closing
sections.summary: Hylak redoes the opening elevator pitch using the full framework, then argues that clear stories—not just great tech—get funded, bought, and talked about. She invites founders to comment with their storytelling challenges.

demonstrations: Opening bad pitch: 'agentic AI orchestration platform for enterprise knowledge retrieval' vs. a wound-first SecOps pitch about exhausted security teams managing disconnected tools.
McDonald's AI drive-thru example reframed as an agent observability pitch: 'If McDonald's had used us, that drive-thru never would have made it to TikTok.'
Before/after support team transformation: 30 minutes digging through docs and tickets versus 10 seconds with one question and sources attached.
Closing elevator-pitch redo: 'Your team is wasting hours digging through Slack, email, and random Excel spreadsheets... We fix that... search it and get the answer you need in seconds.'
limitations: Simple analogies like 'smoke alarm for AI behavior' are not perfect technical definitions—they are front doors to later, deeper conversations.
The framework is optimized for initial pitch clarity, not for the technical due-diligence stage of a sale.
